note.title: Diffusion
note.overview: Explain diffusion as net movement down a concentration gradient and predict how temperature, surface area and gradient affect rate. Apply diffusion to specialised exchange surfaces.

commonMistakes: Diffusion is not “particles moving from high to low” in a single straight direction. Individual particles move randomly; the net movement is down the gradient.
Diffusion does not require energy from respiration.
A partly correct response can still miss a required form, unit, relationship or mark point.
detailedExplanation: This topic is verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Biology Curriculum Outline 2026–27 and the corresponding AQA GCSE Biology 8461 content.

Particles move randomly. If there are more particles in one region than another, more particles will move away from the high-concentration region than move back, creating a net movement down the concentration gradient.
Examples include oxygen diffusing from the alveoli into the blood, carbon dioxide diffusing from blood into alveoli, and urea diffusing from cells into blood plasma.
Factors that increase diffusion rate include a larger concentration gradient, higher temperature and larger surface area. A shorter diffusion distance also improves exchange in biological surfaces.
